title: Shabbetai Tzvi
hook: a would-be messiah stirs the Jewish world, then converts to Islam

segments.voice: Yesterday, 1648: deep mire, whole communities lost, and a number that stands for real people. Today, a hope that rose out of a hard time and swept across the Jewish world.
screen: `A NUMBER THAT STANDS FOR REAL PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: A merchant packs barrels and sends them to his son's house in Hamburg: linen, dried peas, beans, dried meat, all sealed, because any day now word may come to leave for the Land of Israel. His daughter-in-law, Glückel of Hameln, the memoir writer we met not long ago, wrote about those barrels. They sat in her house, packed and waiting, for a long time, while the family went on with ordinary life around them. The news he was waiting for was about one man. Today, his name.
screen: `BARRELS PACKED IN HAMBURG.` → `READY TO LEAVE AT ANY MOMENT.` → `WAITING FOR ONE MAN.`

segments.voice: Shabbetai Tzvi was a scholar from Smyrna, in the Ottoman lands, a man of strange moods and striking presence. A young teacher named Nathan of Gaza declared him the messiah, and Shabbetai, who had hinted at such a claim years before, embraced it. The news traveled by letter, port to port, from the Land of Israel to Amsterdam, Hamburg and Poland. Some communities added prayers for him. Some people sold homes and businesses; others fasted and repented, or danced in the streets. After years of grief, the hope felt close enough to touch. The Hebrew word at the center is mashiach, anointed. In the Tanakh, kings and priests were anointed with oil, and over time the word came to name a king from David's line who would bring the exiles home. Then the Ottoman authorities arrested him. Brought before the sultan's court and given a choice, he converted to Islam. His followers were shocked. Some left him in grief and shame. Some insisted the conversion was a hidden part of his mission, and kept believing. Rabbis who had warned against him from the start were proven right in their own eyes. Jewish tradition calls him a false messiah: not a liar about the hope, but a man whose claim did not come true. The hope itself remained. The prophet Habakkuk had said of the promised vision, "though it tarry, wait for it." The lesson some drew was not to stop waiting, but to wait more carefully.
screen: `NATHAN OF GAZA'S DECLARATION.` · `LETTERS FROM PORT TO PORT.` · `MASHIACH: ANOINTED.` · `BEFORE THE SULTAN'S COURT.` · then, large: `FALSE MESSIAH.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're hoping for right now, something you want badly, and hold it without pushing it away. Then ask two quiet questions: what would it mean to keep this hope even if it takes longer than I want, and what would I lose if I gave up everything else for it today? If you pray, you can bring your hope with you in your own words.
Shabbetai Tzvi. A scholar from Smyrna proclaimed as messiah, who stirred Jewish communities everywhere his letters reached, and then converted to Islam. Today's word.
Your line: false messiah. A hope can outlast a broken promise. Day nine hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Traditional Jewish daily prayer still asks for the coming of the messiah, and Jewish tradition remembers Shabbetai Tzvi as a warning to hope carefully and to test such claims.
